title: The PRD Section Everyone Skips (And Regrets Mid-Sprint)
description:
Most last-minute sprint blowups trace back to one missing paragraph: the non-goals section of the PRD. This Short walks a real mini-PRD and shows why explicitly writing "this will NOT support X" prevents the most common scope-creep argument. A blank non-goals section isn't clean scope, it's a warning sign.

Source lesson(s):
- https://sigilipelli.github.io/product-manager-mastery-path/level-1/05-writing-requirements/

#Shorts

beats.narration: Every argument that blows up a sprint at the last minute starts the same way. Someone assumed a feature was in scope, because nobody ever wrote down that it wasn't.

display.heading: Non-Goals
display.subheading: Writing Requirements -- PM Mastery Path, Level 1

beats.narration: Here's a mini product doc. Goals up top, sure. But look at the non-goals section. It states, plainly, what this release will not do: no multi-person comparison view, no saved filter presets.

display.code:
# Reports filter -- mini-PRD

## Goals
- Reduce time-to-find-one-person's-data to under 15 seconds (baseline: ~4 min)
- No regression in overall reports-page load time

## Non-goals
- Multi-person comparison view (tracked separately as a Level 2 candidate)
- Saving named/custom filter presets (out of scope for v1)

## Open questions
- Should the filter support multi-select in v1, or is single-select enough to validate first?

beats.narration: That's not padding. Every item there is something a reasonable teammate might assume you're building. Writing this will NOT support X kills the argument before it can happen.

display.heading: Non-goals earn their place in every PRD
display.subheading: They prevent the single most common late-sprint argument.

beats.narration: So a blank non-goals section isn't clean scope. It's a red flag that the scope hasn't actually been thought through yet.

display.heading: A blank non-goals section is a red flag
display.subheading: Scope creep starts where the exclusions should have been.
